stem: A patient presents to the ER after a penetrating chest injury. He has a tracheal deviation to the left side with hyperresonance and absent breath sounds in the right hemithorax. What is management?

opts.t: Chest tube without needle decompression on the left side
Needle decompression in the second intercostal space mid clavicular line on the left side
Needle decompression in the second intercostal space mid clavicular line on the right side

srcNote: Source note (Final 442 A Q18): The related immediate-management question keys "A. Needle decompression followed by chest tube". Source note (Midterm 429 F Q50): Clinicians first assess and stabilize the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation, in that order (ABCs, ie, primary survey). The one caveat to this principle in patients with respiratory distress following chest trauma is that breathing may take priority over airway. If the patient is in respiratory distress due to a tension pneumothorax, the clinician should relieve the pneumothorax before performing endotracheal intubation, if needed. Positive pressure ventilation following intubation will exacerbate a pneumothorax. -UpToDate Source note (Midterm 433 A Q2): unstable patients with traumatic pneumothorax: needle thoracostomy (failed?) > finger thoracostomy > (consider chest tube for bilateral pneumothorax , patient requires mechanical ventilation or doesn’t meet pneumothorax stability criteria) - AMBOSS
expl: Tracheal deviation AWAY from the right side + right hyperresonance and absent breath sounds = right tension pneumothorax → immediate needle decompression on the RIGHT (2nd ICS MCL), then chest tube. No X-ray first.

why.D: Never wait for a CXR in tension pneumothorax.

stem: A 30-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. A chest tube is inserted for hemothorax, draining 1800 mL of blood immediately. What is the next best step?

opts.t: Continue chest tube drainage and observe

srcNote: Source note (Final 442 A Q16; Midterm 439 A Q14): Related versions describe 1600 mL of immediate chest-tube drainage and key emergent thoracotomy.
expl: 1800 mL drained immediately (> 1.5 L) = massive haemothorax → urgent thoracotomy in the operating room.

why.A: Observing a massive bleed risks irreversible shock.
why.B: A second tube doesn't stop the bleeding.
why.D: An emergency-department thoracotomy is a resuscitative procedure for the patient in traumatic arrest.

stem: A 20-year-old tall, thin male presents with mild chest pain and shortness of breath. He is hemodynamically stable and has no significant past medical history. Chest X-ray shows a small-sized right apical pneumothorax without mediastinal shift. What is the most appropriate management?
expl: A small primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a stable young patient → high-flow oxygen and observation (oxygen speeds reabsorption of pleural air ~4-fold); repeat the X-ray. Needle aspiration or a drain only if large or symptomatic.

why.A: Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax.
why.B: A chest tube is for moderate/large or symptomatic pneumothorax.

stem: A 28-year-old male presents with a large spontaneous pneumothorax. A chest tube is inserted, but the lung fails to re-expand. The patient is hemodynamically stable and there is a persistent air leak noted through the chest tube. What is the most appropriate next step?
srcNote: AorB Ambiguous source key: the original states "AorB" and does not select one answer.
expl: No key in the source. This year's thoracic notes (Dr. Alghamdi) give exactly this "classic scenario": chest tube in, the lung fails to re-expand and there is a continuous major air leak → suspect a tracheobronchial (airway) injury → next step BRONCHOSCOPY to define it (another or bigger tube won't fix an airway disruption). Book note: for a purely spontaneous pneumothorax, guidelines first check the tube and add suction, then VATS if the leak persists after 3–5 days — but the lecture's answer is bronchoscopy.

why.A: Book first step for a persistent leak in spontaneous pneumothorax; the lecture's scenario points to an airway injury instead.
why.C: A larger tube doesn't treat a major airway leak.
why.D: Not before defining the injury in a stable patient.

stem: A young boy comes to the emergency department after returning from a gym. He has no prior medical history or known lung disease. Imaging reveals a pneumothorax. What is the most likely type of pneumothorax in this case?
expl: A pneumothorax in a young person with no lung disease and no trauma = primary spontaneous pneumothorax (ruptured apical bleb), often in tall thin males and after exertion.

why.B: Secondary needs underlying lung disease (COPD, CF).

opts.t: 4th intercostal space above 5th rib midaxillary line

srcNote: (Practical Procedures & Investigation of Surgical Patients) Source locations differ across versions; the original keys are reported below without choosing a replacement key. Source note (Final 428 Q10 (p. 302)): The related version keys "d. midaxillary line 5th intercostal space". Other source key (Final 429 A Q72 (p. 292)): C. Mid-axillary line, 6th intercostal space. Answer: C (Chest trauma). Source note (Midterm 435 A Q18): The landmark version keys "A. Level of nipple". the Q was about the location of the tube (5th intercostal in the mid-to-anterior axillary line= nipple in males, inframammary line in females)
expl: Chest tube: 4th/5th intercostal space, above the rib (to spare the neurovascular bundle under the rib above), between the anterior and mid-axillary lines.

why.B: Below the rib injures the neurovascular bundle.

stem: A 35 y/o male presented to your emergency department after being stabbed in the chest, on inspection the patient has an isolated stab wound in the right side of the chest. His vital signs are as follows: BP: 80/40 mmHg, pulse 130/min, RR 32/min. Glasgow coma scale is 15/15. What is the most appropriate initial step in his management?
srcNote: (Trauma) Source note (Midterm 439 B Q7): A related stable stab-wound case describes a small pneumothorax and moderate effusion on CXR; its source key is "A. chest tube". Source note (Midterm 435 F Q12): A stab wound presentation is most likely indicative of hemothorax which requires immediate chest tube insertion Source note (Final 434 F Q23 (p. 173)): The abbreviated version states "Answer: A? Incomplete Q" for "Insert chest tube." Its uncertainty is retained here.
expl: Right chest stab with shock (BP 80/40) — massive haemothorax/pneumothorax → chest tube (if signs of tension, needle first). The source: a stab wound most likely causes a haemothorax needing an immediate chest tube.

stem: After oesophagectomy, the surgical drain puts out ~700 mL of serous fluid, which increases and turns white after oral intake. What is the likely cause?
srcNote: Incomplete choice set: option A is "??" and options C and D are blank in the source. The drain volume is written as "700? ml". Source note (Final 436 A Q16): Answer: B, answer is confirmed when Q was reviewed with the course organiser
expl: After oesophagectomy, drainage that turns milky white once oral (fat) intake starts = chyle leak from thoracic duct injury (chylothorax). Confirmed by the course organiser.
ansText: Thoracic duct injury → chylothorax. Milky fluid appears once fat is eaten (chylomicrons; triglycerides > 110 mg/dL). Treat: NPO/TPN or medium-chain-triglyceride diet ± octreotide; re-operate to ligate the duct if output stays high.

stem: A 22 year old male patient had a previous episode of pneumothorax and was managed with a chest tube. Presents again with a pneumothorax picture. Currently on the chest tube and lung is hyperinflated on imaging what is best management?
expl: A recurrent (second) spontaneous pneumothorax is an indication for definitive surgery: VATS bullectomy/blebectomy + pleurodesis, which cuts the recurrence rate to a few percent.

why.A: Bleomycin is a sclerosant for malignant effusions.
why.B: Chemical (talc) pleurodesis via the tube is for patients unfit for surgery.
why.C: A chest tube alone leaves a high recurrence risk.

stem: A patient presented in the ER with tension pneumothorax undergoing, which of the following is irrelevant?

opts.t: Confirm the chest tube insertion with CT
insert at the level of the nipple, midaxillary
low pressure volume can be useful sometimes

srcNote: (practical procedures and investigation of surgical patient) Incomplete stem: the wording ends with "undergoing," before the question. Original wording and key are retained.
expl: Chest-tube placement is confirmed with a chest X-ray, not CT. Asepsis, the 5th ICS at nipple level in the mid-axillary line, and low-pressure suction when needed are all relevant.

stem: Which of the following in not an indication for chest tube insertion?
expl: Chest tubes drain the pleural space (pneumothorax, haemothorax, chylothorax, empyema). Pneumoperitoneum is in the abdomen.

stem: When inserting a chest tube which one of the following is done?

opts.t: A tube size of 12-14 Fr is commonly used for adults

expl: Chest-tube insertion is a sterile procedure under local anaesthesia; adult trauma tubes are large (28–32 Fr for haemothorax); CT isn't needed.

stem: Man presented to the emergency department with Gunshot wound in his chest. Ex: reveals singal sucking chest wound in right side below nippels. BP: 70/30. Puls: 140, RR:40, GCS: 15/15. What is the most appropriate initial step?
srcNote: ( Chest trauma) Source note (Midterm 431 F Unnumbered item 1 after Q7): open chest wound can cause open pneumothorax which requires a 3-sided dressing prior to giving oxygen and prior to placing a chest tube
expl: Keyed three-sided dressing: a sucking chest wound is first sealed with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides (a flutter valve), then a chest tube is placed. With BP 70/30 the chest tube follows immediately (and intubation if he can't maintain his airway/ventilation).

why.A: The definitive next step after sealing the wound.
